paras: The threatened lynching of William Springer was talk among citizens of Colton and San Bernardino, California, of lynching Springer after he was accused of murdering his bride in a Colton hotel around the turn of 1887. Springer was never found alive, and nearly two years later hunters found his skeleton north of San Bernardino with a revolver and a bullet hole in the head. The lynch talk is known only from a San Francisco Call retrospective reprinted when his remains were found in November 1888.

According to the Call, Springer married Katherine Handorff, a former hotel servant of about 20 known as Katie Handorff of Livermore, on 28 December 1886, and the couple traveled by way of San Pedro to Colton, where they took a room at the Transcontinental Hotel. The Call described Springer as a native of Germany who had used several aliases and had kept a saloon at Lodi.

When the couple did not come down by noon, a chambermaid opened the room and found the woman dead on the bed, her head struck with a hammer and nearly severed, the baggage ransacked and her papers and clothing set on fire. Springer was gone, and the Call reported that local citizens were "terribly wrought up," buried the body and set out to search for him, "freely talking of lynching Springer if he could be found." Captain Lees and other detectives found no trace of him, and several men arrested elsewhere in the state were cleared.

In early November 1888 hunters found a skeleton in the hills north of San Bernardino, dressed in a black suit like Springer's and carrying his gold watch and his wife's purse and watch. A revolver lay in the right hand and a bullet hole ran through the head, and a San Bernardino dispatch concluded that "he suicided immediately after the murder." An inquest was announced for 8 November, but no report of its finding appears in the coverage.

The surviving coverage is from the white press of 1888 and concerns the finding of the remains rather than the earlier lynch talk. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union headlined its dispatch "Met His Dueserts [Deserts]," calling Springer "the Colton Wife-Murderer," while the Los Angeles Daily Herald ran "A Mystery Cleared Up" and "Springer's Skeleton." Two days later the Herald reprinted the Call's "Springer's Bones," which mentioned the lynch talk without comment and said that his "whole history is bad."

Reports differ on the date of the murder, given as just after the December 1886 wedding by the Call, as January 1887 by the Herald and as "about two years ago" by the Sacramento dispatch. They also place the remains two, six or about eight miles from San Bernardino.

bases: The only violent act aimed at Springer in the coverage is talk of lynching him by citizens of Colton and San Bernardino while he was a fugitive after the murder (A4); no crowd gathered and he was never found alive (A1, A3).

Citizens only talked of lynching Springer if he could be found (A4); his skeleton was found nearly two years later with a revolver and a bullet wound, and a dispatch called it suicide (A2, A3), so no one was killed by a group.
The murder and the finding of Springer's remains are reported by several papers (A1, A2, A3, A4), but the lynch talk appears only in the S. F. Call retrospective reprinted by the Herald (A4).

accounts.label: S. F. Call retrospective
accounts.gist: After the hotel murder, Colton and San Bernardino citizens searched for Springer, 'freely talking of lynching' him if found; detectives failed to trace him.

accounts.label: San Bernardino dispatches
accounts.gist: Hunters found Springer's skeleton with the murdered woman's effects, a pistol and a bullet hole in the head; one dispatch concluded he killed himself right after the murder.

framing.detail: The Sacramento Daily Record-Union headlined the find 'Met His Dueserts [Deserts]' and called Springer 'the noted murderer'.
The Los Angeles Daily Herald ran it as 'A Mystery Cleared Up' and reported suicide without question.
The reprinted Call piece, 'Their Discovery Revives the Story of His Awful Crime', mentioned the lynch talk without comment and condemned Springer's character.

conflicts.note: The Call retrospective gives the most detail (wedding date, travel), but no contemporary 1886-87 report was found.
